No, spread conditions and ignition causes are fundamentally distinct concepts in fire science. An ignition cause is the specific source or event that initially starts combustion, such as a lightning strike, electrical fault, equipment spark, or deliberate human action. In contrast, spread conditions are the ambient environmental and physical factors—including fuel moisture, air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed, and local topography—that determine how quickly and intensely a fire propagates once it is already burning [K5]. 

Environmental factors like high heat, dry fuels, and strong winds explain why a fire escalates rapidly or crosses firebreaks, but they do not initiate the fire themselves [K5]. result.text: **Fire-count synchronization (2026-11-14, `antonio-rama`).** EQM/GPD harmonizes the *magnitude* of co-observed detections, but the *number* of detected fires is not synchronized across the record: VIIRS joined in 2012 and its constellation grew in 2018 (NOAA-20) and 2023 (NOAA-21), each step revealing more small fires (in 2013–2022 VIIRS detects 1.9–4.2× as many cell-days as Aqua). All-sensor cell-day counts therefore break at 2012 (Chow p 0.002–0.018 in four regions) and correlate poorly with burned area. A ratio correction learned on 2013–2018 predicted 2019–2025 all-sensor counts with 25–30% median error, because the target itself changes with the constellation. The only instrument family observing every year 2000–2026 is MODIS (Terra + Aqua), so script 05's scientific record (`reference_daily`) counts only MODIS-detected cell-days: synchronized by construction, with no estimation. VIIRS still contributes its EQM-harmonized value to the cell-day mean when it co-observes. A cell-day is *spreading* when an H3 R7 neighbour was MODIS-detected the previous day (VIIRS-only neighbours ignored, so spread is synchronized too). Per-cell cube values are unchanged; an earlier detection-completeness factor that scaled pre-2012 totals was superseded, and writing such a factor into cube cells lowered the API's mean-density Chow p (Chilecito 0.35 → 0.08, Iberia 0.013 → 0.001), so it is not used.

request.user_question: What is the difference between FRP in MW and energy in GJ?

conversation.content: What is the difference between FRP in MW and energy in GJ?

Fire Radiative Power (FRP), expressed in megawatts, represents the instantaneous rate of radiant heat output captured at the exact moment of a satellite overpass [K1]. It reflects snapshot thermal intensity consistent with probable active burning rather than cumulative output, and an elevated measurement alone does not officially confirm or name a specific wildfire event [K1]. 

In contrast, total energy, expressed in gigajoules, represents Fire Radiative Energy integrated across time [K1]. Simply adding instantaneous satellite power samples does not yield energy; calculating integrated energy requires temporal modeling over grid cells to account for diurnal progression and gaps between satellite observations [K1]. While instantaneous radiative power indicates immediate combustion strength, integrated radiative energy measures cumulative thermal output, serving as the basis for estimating total dry biomass consumed [K1] [K6].
Can I multiply detection counts by MW to get GJ?

No, you cannot multiply detection counts by megawatts (MW) to obtain energy in gigajoules (GJ). Detection counts simply indicate how many satellite pixels flagged thermal activity, while MW measures instantaneous Fire Radiative Power (FRP), equivalent to megajoules per second (MJ/s), captured at a single satellite overpass [K1]. Because MW is an instantaneous rate, calculating Fire Radiative Energy (FRE) requires integrating power across the duration of the burn over time, rather than multiplying by the number of detected pixels [K1]. 

Furthermore, pixel detection counts vary significantly between sensors due to spatial resolution, sensitivity, and differing overpass schedules—such as 375 m VIIRS versus 1 km MODIS—and do not reflect continuous physical time [K3]. Raw counts cannot serve as a multiplier for energy calculations; scientific energy estimates rely on calibrated FRE integrated over time rather than pixel counts [K1] [K3].
